  "text": "## Cerebrolysin and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in patients with traumatic brain injury: a three-arm randomized trial

## Introduction
Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a significant public health issue that affects millions of individuals worldwide, resulting in long-term disabilities that can affect thinking ability, emotional, behavioral, and personality disturbances, as well as other functional deficits ([Coronado et al., 2015]; [Chan et al., 2022]). Unfortunately, despite advancements in medical care, many individuals with TBI experience significant impairments in cognitive and physical functioning. These impairments can have a major impact on the individual’s quality of life and their ability to return to work and participate in social activities. Therefore, there is a pressing need for innovative interventions that can improve outcomes for these individuals ([Maas et al., 2022]).

We hypothesized that one potential approach to improve outcomes in traumatic brain injury (TBI) patients is combining Cerebrolysin treatment with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). Cerebrolysin is a peptide mixture derived from purified porcine brain proteins that has been shown to have neuroprotective and neurotrophic effects, as it may help protect and regenerate brain cells. After an acute brain lesion, there is always an endogenous continuous brain defense response consisting of two main sequences: an immediate one that aims to reduce brain damage, known as neuroprotection, and a later one that aims to repair the brain damage, known as neurorecovery. Neurotrophic factors are the most important endogenous molecules in brain protection and recovery. They modulate molecules with immediate pleiotropic neuroprotective activity and long-term multimodal effects ([Muresanu et al., 2019]). Due to this unique therapeutic effect, the principle of treatment with neurotrophic factors is based on repetitive periods of treatment in addition to acute administration. Cerebrolysin has a neurotrophic factor-like activity based on the four crucial endogenous neurobiological processes: neurotrophicity, neuroprotection, neuroplasticity, and neurogenesis. Additionally, this activity may have similar effects as the natural sequence of endogenous post-lesional regulation ([Muresanu, 2009]).

Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non-invasive technique that uses magnetic fields to stimulate specific brain areas. Transcranial magnetic stimulation operates on Faraday’s principle of electromagnetic induction. Studies have shown the beneficial role of rTMS in neurorehabilitation, including motor recovery, spasticity reduction, depression treatment, and speech rehabilitation in TBI patients ([Fitzgerald et al., 2009]; [Bonnì et al., 2014]; [Lüdemann-Podubecká et al., 2015]; [Chou et al., 2020]). Although the effects of rTMS on cognition are based on the idea that stimulating different frequencies on a specific area can activate or deactivate specific regions or even networks and thus enhance or inhibit specific functions, experimental studies have also shown that rTMS can influence the molecular and cellular level, which can be independent of the induction of action potentials. One of the critical targets of rTMS for improving cognitive function was presumed to be the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), as magnetic stimulation was thought to have a stimulating effect on its genetic expression. However, this hypothesis could not be confirmed when looking at serum BDNF levels after rTMS ([Jiang and He, 2019]).

While rTMS has been extensively studied for cognitive rehabilitation in other diseases, there is limited and mixed research on its efficacy for cognitive rehabilitation in TBI ([Pink et al., 2021]). The main area of concern regarding the use of TMS in stroke or TBI patients has been the triggering of kindling activity, which can induce seizures. Seizure induction, however, has rarely been reported following rTMS, and animal studies have shown no clear evidence that rTMS leads to increased seizure susceptibility ([Miniussi and Rossini, 2011]). While cognitive treatment with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been tested in Alzheimer’s disease, the combination of rTMS and cognitive treatment appears to benefit cognition ([Bentwich et al., 2011]). However, limited data is available regarding the efficacy of rTMS as an add-on to pharmacological treatment in cognitive rehabilitation ([Haffen et al., 2012]; [Maas et al., 2022]). Studies on rTMS as an add-on treatment for depression had shown promising results when high-frequency magnetic stimulation was used. However, further research is needed to determine the optimal frequency, intensity, and duration of rTMS treatment to improve cognitive outcomes in TBI rehabilitation ([Wei et al., 2017]).

This trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of combining Cerebrolysin treatment with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI). This study represented the first investigation into the effectiveness of combined rTMS and pharmacological intervention (CRB) for cognitive rehabilitation in TBI. Its multi-arm design was aimed to identify which intervention or combination of interventions is most effective while also allowing for a comparison of the individual effects of each intervention. The primary objective of this clinical study was to explore the feasibility, efficacy, and safety of combining rTMS and Cerebrolysin treatment versus CRB alone on a battery of co-primary neurocognitive outcomes at 3 and 6 months after TBI.

## Materials and methods
This study was a phase II, single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study conducted as part of doctoral studies in Cluj-Napoca, Romania. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Iuliu Hatieganu University of Medicine and Pharmacy (8 Babeş Street, 400012 Cluj-Napoca, Romania; +40-264-597-256; contact@umfcluj.ro) on 01/02/2018, reference no. 2/08.01.2018. The protocol was amended on 171/02.04.2018 (ref. no. 133/15.03.2018) and on 30/05/2019 (ref. no. 118/23.04.2019), extending the inclusion criteria and study end date to facilitate the inclusion of patients. The trial followed the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment. The protocol and subsequent trial information may be found in the ISRCTN clinical trial registry ([ISRCTN, n.d.]). The manuscript is reported in line with the extended version of the CONSORT 2010 statement on reporting of multi-arm parallel-group randomized trials ([Juszczak et al., 2019]).

Participants were recruited between April 2018 and September 2021 from patients with moderate-severe TBI aged between 18 and 70 years who had an onset of TBI within 30 days before screening. All patients with TBI were initially admitted to hospital, they were evaluated by clinicians and followed standard treatment. Study visits and study treatment administration lasted 180 days and were conducted in an outpatient setting at the RoNeuro Institute for Neurological Research and Diagnostic, Cluj-Napoca, Romania. Participants were excluded if they had any contraindication to rTMS or Cerebrolysin treatment. The trial inclusion criteria consisted of patients with traumatic brain injury onset within 30 days before screening, CT/MRI-confirmed focal or diffuse lesions, age 18–70 years (updated 28/02/2020: 18–80 years), Pre-Trauma Karnofsky Index 100, and willingness to comply with the protocol requirements for the duration of the study. Patients with metal implants in the head or within the stimulation area, medical implanted devices (cardiac pacemaker, cochlea implant or medication pumps), history of intracranial interventions, evidence of pre-existing major health problems (e.g., cancer, hematological, renal, hepatic, or coronary disease, psychiatric disorder, diabetes, myocardial infarction or other known heart diseases, disabling or musculoskeletal problems like rheumatoid arthritis, epilepsy, evidence of degenerative or inflammatory diseases affecting nervous system), history of intracranial interventions, any neurological or non-neurological condition independent from TBI that might influence the functional outcome or other efficacy outcome measures, injury of writing hand influencing cognitive or other outcome measures, clear clinical signs of intoxication influencing the evaluation, major drug dependency including alcohol, chronic treatment with steroids, Ca2 + -channel blockers or major anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin and other coumarin derivates), monoamine oxidase inhibitors, antipsychotic drugs or nootropic molecules, patients with penetrating brain injury, females who are pregnant or lactating, or females who are of childbearing potential and not taking adequate contraceptive precautions were excluded from the study. Females of childbearing potential taking acceptable contraceptive precautions were included in the study.

The study schedule consisted of three visits for each participant: Screening and Baseline at Study Day 30, Visit 1 at Study Day 101, and Visit 2 at Study Day 180. There was no follow-up conducted after the 180-day evaluation. Patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria were assigned a random number based on a pre-generated list by a third-party service (blocks of three, equal allocation to groups). Sealed and opaque randomization envelopes were provided to the study center based on the random list, the person responsible for preparing the ready-to-use infusion, the person administering the rTMS protocol, and the study coordinator. Participants were randomly allocated to one of three groups: (1) Cerebrolysin and rTMS–CRB + rTMS, (2) Cerebrolysin and sham rTMS - CRB + SHM, or (3) placebo and sham rTMS–PLC + SHM. All groups received standard care after traumatic brain injury. All participants received three cycles of treatment. The first group received 30 ml of Cerebrolysin infusions + rTMS for 10 days at Days 31–40, 61–70, and 91–100. The second group received 30 ml of Cerebrolysin infusions + sham rTMS for the same duration and days as the first group, while the third group received a placebo of 250 ml of 0.9% saline solution + sham rTMS for the same duration and days as the other groups. The Cerebrolysin was diluted in 0.9% saline solution up to 250 ml, and the rTMS stimulation parameters for left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) were 10 Hz (10 stimuli/second), 1,200 stimuli/day, with a total session time of 33 min–40 trains of 3 sec interleaved by a pause of 20 s, and an intensity of 120% of resting motor threshold. The resting motor threshold was determined at the beginning of the first treatment session and was defined as the minimal intensity at which at least five of 10 motor-evoked potentials were 50 μV in amplitude in the pollicis abductor brevis. Repetitive stimulation was delivered using the medical device MagPro X100 (MagVenture, Farum, Denmark) with a figure-8 coil (MCF-B65), held tangential to the scalp with the handle pointing upward. The DLPFC was localized using the 10–20 EEG system, with the coil at F3. Sham stimulation was performed with a sham-coil (MCF-P-B 65, MagVenture, Farum, Denmark) with a mechanical outline and sound level identical to MCF-B65, providing the same cutaneous discomfort and muscle twitching level as real stimulation. Two rTMS technicians administered both sham and real rTMS without being involved in any other study-related procedures or allowed to disclose information about the treatment procedure.

The primary outcome measures consisted of 10 cognitive function tests, which were assessed by a team of neuropsychologists using the Stroop Color-Word Test ([Scarpina and Tagini, 2017]), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) ([Hobson, 2015]), two subscales of the Wechsler adult intelligence scale (3rd edition): Processing Speed Index (PSI) and Digit Span ([Wechsler, n.d.]), Trail Making Test ([Bucks, 2013]), three subscales of the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB): One Touch Stockings of Cambridge, The Multitasking Test, and Reaction Time ([Sandberg, 2011]), the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HARS) ([Hamilton, 1959]) and the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HDRS) ([Hamilton, 1960]). These tests were conducted on days 30, 101, and 180 of the study. Adverse events of the interventions were recorded using a safety report form based on patient self-reports during the entire duration of the trial. Secondary outcomes consisted of eye movements assessed using a Tobii Pro TX300 eye-tracking device and brain electrical activity assessed using electroencephalography (EEG). Since these secondary measures require distinct data processing and specialized analysis, they will be reported in subsequent manuscripts.

The trial was conducted under double-blind conditions to ensure the blinding of investigators, study personnel, and patients to treatment allocation. To maintain blinding, colored infusion lines were used for drug administration as Cerebrolysin is an amber-colored solution. Patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria were assigned a random number corresponding to the pre-generated random list prepared by a biometrician selected by the sponsor. Each patient received a set of envelopes for their treatment, which was distributed to the study nurse responsible for preparing the infusion solution. The study nurse was only responsible for the preparation and administration of infusion solutions and was not involved in any other study-related procedures or allowed to disclose information about treatment allocation. The treatment envelope was not opened until the patient’s first ready-to-use infusion was prepared. The database was closed, and analysis populations were determined before unblinding the whole study.

The study’s power was determined based on certain specifications. These included a one-sided type I error of alpha = 0.05, a type II error of β = 0.2, and a medium-sized effect size according to Cohen. The estimated correlations among the outcome scales were ρ = 0.4. Sample size calculations were performed using non-parametric methods with the Nnpar 1.0 software from idv Data Analysis and Study Planning. The total required sample size for the study was determined to be 30 patients per group, including a 10% enhancement for potential dropouts. This sample size allows for the detection of a medium-sized difference between groups with an 80% power. Due to the exploratory nature of this trial, aimed to test the feasibility and safety of the concomitant intervention, interim power calculations or extensions of the trials were not performed.

Before unblinding the study, a blind review was conducted, in which protocol violations were classified as “severe,” “major,” “minor,” or “none,” and patients were allocated to individual data sets based on the classification of possible protocol violations. The analysis populations included safety, intention-to-treat (ITT), and per protocol (PP). The safety population included all patients who received at least one dose of study medication and had at least one contact with the investigator afterward. The ITT population was defined as all patients who had no “severe” violation of entry criteria, received at least one dose of medication, and had at least one post-baseline observation of at least one primary efficacy criterion (“modified” ITT). The PP population included all patients who were eligible for ITT evaluation and did not show major protocol deviations. A sensitivity analysis was performed for the PP data set as an exploratory approach. Homogeneity analyses for baseline were performed based on the ITT population. In case of heterogeneities, stratified analyses were performed as second-line analyses. Patients with compliance for the entire study below 80% for the treatments were considered protocol violators and were not included in the per protocol analysis. Based on good clinical practice recommendations on the conduct of clinical trials during the COVID-19 pandemic, the study team decided to delay study visits rather that terminate the study. Visit delays during the 2020 lockdown (n = 16; 15 for Visit 2, 1 for Visit 3) were included in the PP analysis, provided they did not have other violations. Due to the low sample size, any sensitivity analysis excluding these cases would not bring additional information.

Statistical procedures were performed using the R programming language and SAS® On Demand for Academics ([Ogle et al., n.d.]). Descriptive statistics and graphs were generated for the ITT population. We performed the Kruskal-Wallis Rank Sum Test for both ITT and PP populations to assess the statistical significance of the differences across groups. The pairwise comparisons were performed using Dunn’s test for multiple comparisons with Bonferroni adjustment. Safety analyses were conducted on the ITT population and included the incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events.

The primary analysis compared the three groups’ baseline changes in composite neurocognitive outcomes. All variables were included in the Kruskal-Wallis analysis. For each patient, we calculated the differences between Visit 1 (Day 101) and baseline and Visit 2 (Day 180) and baseline across all variables and used z-scores to create a composite cognitive total score ([Andrade, 2021]).

## Results
The study enrolled 93 individuals who had suffered traumatic brain injury 30 days before screening. The ITT population, used for all efficacy analyses, included patients with at least one dose of medication and at least one post-baseline observation of at least one primary efficacy criterion. The PP population was defined as all patients eligible for ITT evaluation and who did not show significant protocol deviations. Violation of inclusion or exclusion criteria was not observed in the sample. Premature discontinuations were reported in 9 patients due to loss to follow-up (9.6%). The ITT population is comprised of 86 TBI patients.

In contrast, the PP population comprises 84 patients (loss to follow-up from ITT–CRB + SHM: 1, PLC + SHM: 1). The safety population included all patients with at least one dose of study medication and one subsequent contact with study investigators (86 patients). Study populations were comparable in gender distribution, which was unbalanced at a 4:1 male-to-female ratio (Figure 1). The composite outcome analysis is based on the ITT set without missing data (n = 64).

The group with the highest mean age was CRB + SHM (mean = 55.46 years), followed by PLC + SHM (mean = 51.04 years), and CRB + rTMS (mean = 49.87 years). Boxplots of age distribution across study groups (Figure 2).

In total, 21 adverse events (AE) were reported during this trial for 7 patients in the CRB + SHM group, 6 in the CRB + rTMS group, and 8 in the PLC + SHM group. Among adverse events, we remarked symptoms related to the traumatic brain injury itself or other associated health conditions, Covid infections, and other types of infections. Also, for 4 patients there were reported certain symptoms, like headache, dizziness, or fatigue, already associated in the literature with Cerebrolysin administration or rTMS. Nevertheless, they were described as mild symptoms, they did not require concomitant treatment or interruption of study medication, and the outcome was favorable. One serious adverse event (SAE) was reported for the CRB + SHM group. Based on the assessment of study investigators, the SAE was not related to the administration of the intervention. Non-parametric group differences were not statistically significant (Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared = 0.57734, df = 2, p-value = 0.7493 for AE, and Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared = 2.0714, df = 2, p-value = 0.355 for SAE). Results from post-hoc Dunn’s test for multiple comparisons for both AE and SAE are available in Table 1.

Composite outcomes in the ITT population for Visit 2 and Visit 3 were compiled based on z-scores of each outcome scale baseline differences (n = 64: PLC + SHM: 24, CRB + SHM:20, CRB + rTMS:20, less than the total sample size due to missing data). The Kruskal–Wallis test conducted to compare the scores of three groups on the composite cognitive outcome revealed no significant differences among the groups (Day 101–χ² = 5.732, p = 0.06; Day 180 χ² = 5.833, p = 0.54). The three groups included participants who received CRB + rTMS, CRB + SHM, and PLC + SHM interventions. Results from post-hoc Dunn’s test for multiple comparisons for both Day 101 and Day 180 baseline differences in composite cognitive outcome are available in Table 2. Despite descriptive superiority for both intervention groups, non-parametric tests were not statistically significant for the combined outcome (Figures 3, 4).

## Discussion
The primary aim of this clinical study was to investigate the practicability, effectiveness, and safety of administering rTMS and Cerebrolysin in combination compared to CRB alone. In addition, the study evaluated several co-primary neurocognitive outcomes at 3 and 6 months following TBI. Despite the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, this clinical study was successfully conducted, and data were collected from all participants. The study team implemented various measures, such as antigen screening and specialized protective equipment, to ensure the safety of participants and staff while maintaining the integrity of the study. However, there were delays in some of the in-person visits, which may have impacted the accuracy of the data collected by introducing a disadvantage for active treatment arms as the window for neurorecovery decreases following brain injury ([Bernhardt et al., 2017]). While these limitations were acknowledged in the manuscript, it is also essential to acknowledge the challenges faced by clinical research during the pandemic.

Our findings highlight that the combination of rTMS and Cerebrolysin is safe and well tolerated by patients with traumatic brain injury. While primary outcomes and their subscales did not show statistically significant differences, the descriptive trends in this study support existing literature on the efficacy and safety of both rTMS and Cerebrolysin ([Muresanu et al., 2016]; [Guekht et al., 2017]; [Beghi et al., 2021]; [Pink et al., 2021]; [Mureşanu D. F. et al., 2022]; [Mureşanu I. A. et al., 2022]).

The hypothesis for this study was based on findings of the CAPTAIN trial series ([Poon et al., 2019]; [Muresanu et al., 2020]; [Vester et al., 2021]), which showed a significant effect of Cerebrolysin on a multidimensional ensemble of outcomes in patients who had suffered moderate-severe TBI. While study populations in our trial are similar to the CAPTAIN project, the model of treatment administration is fundamentally different, as interventions are initiated 30 days after injury (i.e., chronic, intermittent admission), as opposed to acute initiation (i.e., 4–6 h after hospital admission). This allowed us to provide insight into the ability of the interventions to operate in patients in the chronic stage of illness. The second important difference between the two projects is the control for TBI severity in the emergency setting. As patients enrolled in our study were included in a third-party outpatient clinic 1 month after acute presentation, information such as admission Glasgow Coma Scale scores (i.e., a key clinical prognostic factor for TBI outcome and neurorehabilitation potential) or other data gathered from the emergency setting were not available. Hence, in contrast with the CAPTAIN trial, which had Baseline Prognostic Risk Score (BPRS) as a tool for baseline comparability, our sample has an unknown distribution of TBI severity, which could have confounded results similar to the age imbalance present between study groups (i.e., the Cerebrolysin and sham group was roughly five years older, on average).

While paradigm-shifting clinical implications based solely on this study cannot be drawn, findings suggest that future studies may show the potential to improve cognitive and motor function in patients with TBI. Based on our observations, limited potential risks are associated with the combined intervention after TBI. These findings align with existing literature ([Bornstein et al., 2018]; [Kim and Paik, 2020]; [Kletzel et al., 2020]; [Strilciuc et al., 2021]). Therefore, both Cerebrolysin and its neuromodulatory enhancement by rTMS should be considered as candidates when deciding a neurorehabilitation strategy for TBI in patients who have access to such interventions. These should also be discussed in clinical guidelines.

Our study also provides valuable epistemological insight into clinical trial methodology in neurotrauma. While lessons from the CAPTAIN trial, such as the importance of multidimensional outcome assessment, have been incorporated into our design, the absence of stratification based on acute severity remains an important feature that should not be omitted in similar work in the future. In addition, other limitations may have further influenced our results, which should also be considered. For example, the sample size was relatively small, and the study was conducted at a single site, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to larger populations. Additionally, our study’s duration was relatively short, and longer-term follow-up studies are necessary to determine the treatment’s long-term efficacy. Additionally, the exclusion of specific patient populations, such as those with more mild TBI or pre-existing medical conditions, may limit the applicability of the findings to these groups. Considering these limitations when interpreting the study’s results and applying them to clinical practice is essential. The study’s strengths include its rigorous design and adherence to Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The blinding procedures minimized the potential for bias in the study’s findings. Using both rTMS and Cerebrolysin allowed for a comprehensive examination of these treatments’ potential benefits and risks in TBI patients.

However, much remains to be learned about the optimal combined use of rTMS and Cerebrolysin. Overall, there is a great need for continued research in this area to understand better the optimal use of such interventions in TBI patients and further improve outcomes for this vulnerable patient population. Multi-center studies with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm the efficacy of rTMS and Cerebrolysin in TBI patients. While the current study provides promising results, more extensive studies with more diverse patient populations are needed to establish the generalizability of these findings. In addition to larger, confirmatory trials that could identify the effect size for the intervention, further studies could explore the optimal dosages and treatment protocols for rTMS and Cerebrolysin, as well as their long-term effects on patients with TBI.

Moreover, future studies could explore potential subgroup effects, such as the effects of rTMS and Cerebrolysin in patients with varying degrees of injury severity or different ages. This information could help to identify which patients are most likely to benefit from these interventions and tailor treatment accordingly. Given that TBI is a complex disorder with a range of cognitive and functional deficits, future research could explore the potential benefits of combining rTMS and Cerebrolysin with other interventions, such as cognitive rehabilitation or pharmacotherapy. This could help maximize these interventions’ potential benefits and improve outcomes for TBI patients.

In conclusion, our study provides preliminary evidence for the safety and potential efficacy of combining rTMS and Cerebrolysin in improving cognitive and functional outcomes in TBI patients. This combined intervention may synergistically promote neuroplasticity and neural repair in TBI patients. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and explore potential subgroup effects. The study’s limitations, such as the small sample size and exclusion of specific patient populations, should also be considered when interpreting the results. Nonetheless, the study’s rigorous design and adherence to Good Clinical Practice guidelines provide confidence in the validity of the findings. This study also highlights the importance of multidisciplinary approaches in TBI rehabilitation and the potential for combining neuropsychological measurements and interventions to optimize patient outcomes.

headline.statement: The trial reports one of its two co-primary cognitive endpoints as p = 0.54, but the paper's own supplementary annex shows the test statistic printed beside it corresponds to a p of roughly 0.054 -- ten times smaller.
headline.evidence: Results: "The Kruskal-Wallis test conducted to compare the scores of three groups on the composite cognitive outcome revealed no significant differences among the groups (Day 101-χ² = 5.732, p = 0.06; Day 180 χ² = 5.833, p = 0.54)." Supplementary Annex 1, same software, same df = 2, brackets that statistic on both sides: "Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 5.7111, df = 2, p-value = 0.05752" and "Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 6.082, df = 2, p-value = 0.04779". Since p falls as chi-squared rises at fixed df, χ² = 5.833 must give p between 0.048 and 0.058. Table 2 corroborates: the Day 180 post-hoc contrast CRB + rTMS-PLC + SHM is Z = 2.2295095, P.unadj = 0.02578002 -- incompatible with an omnibus p of 0.54.
headline.plain: For the six-month cognitive result -- one of the study's two main outcomes -- the paper prints a number meant to show how likely the observed group differences were to be chance. The printed figure says the differences were nowhere near meaningful. But the study's own supplementary file shows that the underlying calculation actually points to a result on the very edge of the conventional cut-off. The most likely explanation is a lost decimal point in typesetting, and the study's overall conclusion of 'no significant difference' still holds either way; but as printed, the paper makes a borderline finding look decisively empty.

findings.title: Day-180 co-primary p-value irreconcilable with the chi-squared printed beside it
findings.location: Results, composite outcome paragraph; cross-referenced against Supplementary Annex 1 and Table 2
findings.reported: "Day 101-χ² = 5.732, p = 0.06; Day 180 χ² = 5.833, p = 0.54", with df = 2 (three groups).
findings.computed: Supplementary Annex 1 prints 44 chi-squared/p pairs from the same software at df = 2. Two bracket the Day-180 statistic: χ² = 5.7111 gives p = 0.05752, and χ² = 6.082 gives p = 0.04779. Because p is strictly decreasing in chi-squared at fixed df, χ² = 5.833 must yield p in (0.04779, 0.05752) -- approximately 0.054, about one tenth of the printed 0.54. The companion Day-101 figure is internally consistent (χ² = 5.732 sits just above 5.7111, so p just under 0.0575 rounds to the printed 0.06), which isolates the defect to the Day-180 value. Table 2's Day-180 row CRB + rTMS-PLC + SHM (Z = 2.2295095, P.unadj = 0.02578002) independently corroborates a borderline omnibus, not a null one.
findings.assumptions: df = 2 is not printed for the composite tests but follows necessarily from three groups, and the paper prints df = 2 for its other Kruskal-Wallis tests. The bracketing values are the paper's own, so no external constraint is imposed. Graded highly_suspicious rather than impossible for one reason only: no validated tool in this kit converts a chi-squared plus df to a p-value, so this rests on bracketing against the paper's printed pairs plus monotonicity rather than on a tool-computed p. The modal benign cause -- a dropped decimal point, 0.054 printed as 0.54 -- is also the likeliest one here.
findings.plain: One of the study's two headline cognitive results, at six months, is reported with a figure suggesting the three treatment groups were about as similar as you could imagine. The study's own supplementary file contains dozens of comparable calculations, and two of them sit on either side of this one -- which pins the correct figure at about a tenth of what was printed, right at the edge of the conventional threshold. A dropped decimal point in typesetting is the most likely cause. The paper's stated conclusion that the groups did not differ significantly survives the correction, but a reader is being shown a decisively empty result where the data actually gave a marginal one.

consequence.explanation: The Day-180 conclusion of 'no significant differences' on a co-primary endpoint survives at the corrected p of about 0.054, but the strength of evidence is misstated by an order of magnitude.

findings.title: Discussion's claim that no subscale reached significance contradicted by the paper's own annex
findings.location: Discussion paragraph 2 and Results final paragraph, versus Supplementary Annex 1 (DS_B_v2-baseline, TMT1_v2-baseline)
findings.reported: "While primary outcomes and their subscales did not show statistically significant differences, the descriptive trends in this study support existing literature..." and, in Results, "Individual outcomes scales are similar to composite findings."
findings.computed: Supplementary Annex 1 reports Digit Span Backward at Day 180 as significant on the omnibus test in both analysis populations -- intention-to-treat χ² = 7.2622, df = 2, p = 0.02649, and per-protocol χ² = 6.082, df = 2, p = 0.04779 -- and the Cerebrolysin + rTMS versus placebo contrast survives the paper's own Bonferroni adjustment in both (adjusted p = 0.0227401 and 0.0423081). Trail Making Test 1 at Day 180 is also significant on the intention-to-treat omnibus (χ² = 6.4319, p = 0.04012). Three results below 0.05 where the text asserts none.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The counterweight must be carried alongside: 2 of 22 intention-to-treat omnibus tests falling below 0.05 is close to the roughly 1.1 expected by chance alone, so the paper's underlying inference of no subscale effect may well be correct even though the sentence describing it is not. The direction is conservative -- the authors understate their own positive findings rather than overstate them.
findings.plain: The paper states twice that none of the individual cognitive tests showed a meaningful difference between treatment groups. Its own supplementary file shows otherwise: one memory test at six months did cross the conventional threshold, in both ways the authors analysed the data, and survived their own adjustment for testing many things at once; a second test crossed it too. Unusually, the error runs against the authors' own interest -- they are underselling a positive result, not overselling one. And with twenty-two comparisons made, finding two by chance is roughly what you would expect, so the paper's overall conclusion may still be right. But the sentence as written does not describe the data behind it.

consequence.explanation: The stated claim that no subscale showed a statistically significant difference is contradicted by three results below 0.05 in the paper's own annex, one of which survives the authors' Bonferroni adjustment in both analysis populations.

findings.title: No baseline characteristics table and no per-arm sample sizes in a CONSORT-reported three-arm trial
findings.location: Whole paper; Methods analysis-populations paragraph; Results paragraphs 1-4
findings.reported: "The manuscript is reported in line with the extended version of the CONSORT 2010 statement on reporting of multi-arm parallel-group randomized trials." Baseline data given anywhere: three mean ages in prose (55.46, 51.04, 49.87 years), a gender bar chart, and an overall 4:1 male-to-female ratio. Analysis populations: 93 enrolled, 86 intention-to-treat, 84 per-protocol, 64 in the composite analysis.
findings.computed: Zero baseline comparison p-values are reported, so the two baseline-integrity checks this toolkit exists to run -- the Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher similarity test and Bayesian Table 1 dispersion -- have no input and could not be run at all. Per-arm randomised, intention-to-treat and per-protocol sample sizes are reported zero times for all three arms; the only per-arm counts anywhere are 24/20/20 within the 64-patient composite subset. The paper pre-specifies that "In case of heterogeneities, stratified analyses were performed as second-line analyses", then acknowledges a heterogeneity in the Discussion -- "the Cerebrolysin and sham group was roughly five years older, on average" -- yet reports no stratified or age-adjusted analysis anywhere.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements; the CONSORT items invoked (15, 13a, 16) are those the paper itself claims to follow.
findings.plain: Randomised trials normally open with a table showing that the treatment groups started out comparable -- age, sex, severity -- and stating how many patients went into each group. This paper has neither, despite saying it follows the reporting standard that requires both. That has two costs. A reader cannot tell whether the randomisation worked or whether patients dropped out unevenly from one arm; and the single most informative check anyone could run on a randomised trial's integrity is unavailable here, so this review is quieter about the trial than it would otherwise be. Separately, the authors planned in advance to re-run their analysis adjusted for any group imbalance, then reported an age gap of about five years between groups -- and the adjusted analysis never appears.

consequence.explanation: The pre-specified stratified analysis triggered by the authors' own acknowledged age imbalance is never reported, so the primary comparison is never adjusted for the one baseline difference they flag.

findings.title: Three of ten stated co-primary instruments feed the composite endpoint but are never individually reported
findings.location: Methods primary-outcome list versus Supplementary Annex 1
findings.reported: "The primary outcome measures consisted of 10 cognitive function tests", including "three subscales of the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB): One Touch Stockings of Cambridge, The Multitasking Test, and Reaction Time". Results direct the reader to the annex for individual outcomes: "Individual outcomes scales are similar to composite findings. More information is available in the Supplementary Annex 1."
findings.computed: Supplementary Annex 1 reports group differences for 11 outcome families covering 7 instruments (MoCA, two Processing Speed subscales, two Stroop derived scores, Digit Span forward and backward, two Trail Making tests, Hamilton depression, Hamilton anxiety). The three CANTAB subscales -- One Touch Stockings, Multitasking Test, Reaction Time -- appear nowhere in the annex or the main text, although their columns are present in the deposited dataset at all three visits (OTS01/OTS02, MTTTC01/MTTTC02, RTISMRT/RTIFMRT) and their z-score transforms contribute to the composite primary endpoint.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. This is a selective-reporting gap, not an arithmetic error.
findings.plain: The study names ten cognitive tests as its main outcomes and combines them all into a single overall score. When it points readers to the supplement for the individual test results, three of those ten -- a planning task, a multitasking task and a reaction-time task -- are simply not there, even though the data were collected at every visit and fed into the combined score. So three measures shaped the headline result while never being shown on their own, and the claim that the individual tests looked like the combined result cannot be checked for them.

consequence.explanation: The claim that individual outcome scales resemble the composite cannot be verified for three of the ten stated co-primary instruments.

findings.title: Visit and instrument labels disagree across the paper, its annex and its deposited dataset
findings.location: Deposited dataset (Harvard Dataverse DOFCIV, sheet 'ITT_analysis set') header row; Figure 3 and Figure 4 captions; Methods versus Supplementary Annex 1
findings.reported: Deposited Visit-3 column block: CWTTM1_3, CWTTM2_3, CWTTM3_3, SCWT_W-D_2, SCWT_C-D_2, DGFRES_3, DGBRES_3 -- the two Stroop derived scores carry the Visit-2 suffix inside the Visit-3 block, as do their z-score companions, so both names appear twice in the header. Figure 3: "...after the second visit on study day 101..."; Figure 4: "...after the second visit on study day 180...". Methods name "the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HARS)"; the annex labels the same outcome "HADS_v1-baseline" and "HADS_v2-baseline"; the dataset column is HARTS.
findings.computed: Two duplicated column names in the Visit-3 block where SCWT_W-D_3 and SCWT_C-D_3 are expected, plus their two mislabelled z-score companions. Two primary-outcome figure captions describing different study days as the same visit. Four incompatible visit-numbering schemes in use across the paper (Methods: Visit 1 = Day 101, Visit 2 = Day 180; Results: Visit 2 and Visit 3; dataset: _1/_2/_3; annex: v1/v2). Three sources naming the anxiety instrument, two agreeing on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale and one naming the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, which is a different instrument with different content and scoring.
findings.assumptions: This establishes a labelling defect, NOT duplicated content: the raw-data duplication scan reported zero repeated column sequences, so the two same-named columns are not verbatim copies of each other. Whether the mislabelled columns hold Visit-2 or Visit-3 values cannot be determined from the naming alone, and warrants clarification rather than any stronger inference. Confidence is medium because the dataset header was read in the sweep and not re-read by me at source in this pass.
findings.plain: The paper, its supplement and its published data file do not agree with each other about which visit is which, or what one of the tests is called. In the data file, two columns in the six-month block are labelled with the three-month suffix, so those names appear twice in the file. That matters because those columns feed the six-month headline score: if the values behind them really are the earlier measurements, the six-month result would be built partly on stale data. The labels alone do not prove that, and the authors could settle it immediately. The two main result figures also both describe their timepoint as 'the second visit' while showing different days, and the anxiety questionnaire is given one name in the methods and a different, genuinely different, questionnaire's name in the supplement.

consequence.explanation: If the mislabelled columns hold Visit-2 values, the Day-180 composite primary endpoint would incorporate two stale measurements; separately, the two primary-outcome figures cannot be mapped to their timepoints from their captions alone.

findings.title: Safety conclusion resting on significance tests of a single serious adverse event
findings.location: Results, adverse events paragraph; Table 1, SAE columns; Discussion paragraph 2
findings.reported: "One serious adverse event (SAE) was reported for the CRB + SHM group... Non-parametric group differences were not statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 0.57734, df = 2, p-value = 0.7493 for AE, and Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 2.0714, df = 2, p-value = 0.355 for SAE)." Table 1 SAE post-hoc Z values: -1.260425, 0.000000, 1.239239, with adjusted p of 0.6225488, 1.0000000, 0.6457706. Discussion: "the combination of rTMS and Cerebrolysin is safe and well tolerated by patients with traumatic brain injury."
findings.computed: The serious-adverse-event variable takes the value 1 for exactly one patient among 86 and 0 for the other 85. A rank-based omnibus test and three post-hoc contrasts on such a variable cannot detect any between-group difference whatever, so p = 0.355 carries no evidential content about comparative safety. The numbers are internally consistent -- the post-hoc Z of exactly 0.000000 with adjusted p = 1.0 correctly reflects two arms with zero events. The paper reports no confidence intervals anywhere, so the largest harm difference still compatible with these data cannot be bounded.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. This is a design and interpretation observation, not an arithmetic error; the arithmetic is correct.
findings.plain: Exactly one serious medical event occurred in the whole trial, among 86 patients. The authors ran statistical tests comparing the three treatment groups on serious events and reported no difference. With a single event, those tests could not have produced any other answer -- they are incapable of detecting a difference, so 'no difference found' tells a reader nothing about whether the combined treatment is riskier. Because the paper reports no ranges of uncertainty anywhere, there is also no way to say how large a real safety difference could still be hiding. The trial's headline claim that the combination is safe and well tolerated rests partly on this.

consequence.explanation: The abstract and Discussion conclusion that the combined intervention is safe and well tolerated rests partly on significance tests that a single event renders uninformative.

findings.title: Stated 80% power at 30 patients per group not reproducible from the stated parameters
findings.location: Materials and methods, power paragraph
findings.reported: "These included a one-sided type I error of alpha = 0.05, a type II error of β = 0.2, and a medium-sized effect size according to Cohen. The estimated correlations among the outcome scales were ρ = 0.4... The total required sample size for the study was determined to be 30 patients per group, including a 10% enhancement for potential dropouts. This sample size allows for the detection of a medium-sized difference between groups with an 80% power."
findings.computed: Recomputed with exact noncentral distributions under the standard reading of a medium effect across three groups (Cohen's f = 0.25, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80): 53 patients per group are required, 159 in total. At the reported 30 per group the achieved power is 0.5396, not 0.80 -- a shortfall of 23 per group. The sweep additionally recomputed the two-group reading (Cohen's d = 0.5), which requires 64 per group and yields achieved power 0.4779, and the tool rejected the one-tailed reading there as well.
findings.assumptions: Stated caveat that must be carried: the paper did not use either of these procedures. It used Nnpar 1.0, a non-parametric multivariate sample-size method pooling information across ten correlated outcome scales at rho = 0.4, and such a method can legitimately require fewer subjects than a univariate test. This is therefore a finding that the published power statement cannot be reproduced from the parameters given, not a demonstration that it is arithmetically wrong. Mitigating context: the paper concedes the point itself -- "Given the low sample size of the trial that would inherently lead to the low power of reported analyses" -- so the underpowering is disclosed rather than hidden.
findings.plain: Before running a trial, researchers calculate how many patients they need to have a fair chance of detecting a real effect. This study says 30 per group gives it an 80% chance of spotting a moderate difference. Redoing that calculation the two standard ways gives 53 and 64 per group; at 30, the realistic chance is closer to 50%. The authors used specialised software for correlated outcomes that can legitimately justify a smaller number, so this is not proof the figure is wrong -- but as published, the calculation cannot be checked or reproduced. To their credit, the authors say elsewhere in the paper that the study was underpowered.

consequence.explanation: The claim that 30 per group affords 80% power to detect a medium effect cannot be reproduced under any standard univariate reading of the stated parameters.

findings.title: Trial registration number absent and protocol amendment record incomplete
findings.location: Materials and methods, paragraph 1, and inclusion criteria paragraph
findings.reported: "The protocol and subsequent trial information may be found in the ISRCTN clinical trial registry ([ISRCTN, n.d.])." "The protocol was amended on 171/02.04.2018 (ref. no. 133/15.03.2018) and on 30/05/2019 (ref. no. 118/23.04.2019)..." Inclusion criteria: "age 18-70 years (updated 28/02/2020: 18-80 years)".
findings.computed: The registry is named but no ISRCTN identifier appears anywhere in the body text, and the citation is undated ('n.d.'), so CONSORT item 23 is not satisfied by a paper that states it follows CONSORT. '171/02.04.2018' is not a well-formed date. Two amendments are listed (2018, 2019) but the inclusion criteria record a third change dated 28/02/2020 raising the upper age limit from 70 to 80 years, corresponding to neither listed amendment.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. No reported statistic depends on these; the cost is to verifiability rather than to any number.
findings.plain: Clinical trials are registered publicly before they start, so that anyone can later check the researchers measured what they said they would. This paper names the registry but never gives the registration number, so that check cannot be done -- including for the adjusted analysis the authors promised in advance and did not report. The record of changes to the study plan is also incomplete: one amendment date is garbled into something that is not a date, and a third change to the eligibility rules, raising the maximum age from 70 to 80, is mentioned in passing without appearing in the list of amendments. Age is the very characteristic the authors later flag as unbalanced between groups.

consequence.explanation: Pre-specification of outcomes and analyses cannot be checked against the registry, so no claim in the paper can be independently confirmed as pre-planned.

findings.title: Dropout percentage flagged by one engine and cleared by the other
findings.location: Results, paragraph 1
findings.reported: "The study enrolled 93 individuals who had suffered traumatic brain injury 30 days before screening... Premature discontinuations were reported in 9 patients due to loss to follow-up (9.6%)."
findings.computed: Our grim_percentage returned `impossible`: read as a share of 93, 9.6% implies a count of 8.928, and the attainable percentages either side are 8.6 and 9.7 -- 9 of 93 being 9.677%, which rounds to 9.7. The mandatory R cross-check disagreed: R `scrutiny` returned `consistent` for mean = 9.6, n = 93, 1 decimal. The two engines are answering different questions -- `scrutiny` has no share mode, so it tested 9.6 as a mean of 93 integer observations (attainable, since 892/93 rounds to 9.6) rather than as a share of the form 100k/93. Per the rulebook, an engine disagreement means our tooling is at issue rather than the paper, and a cross-check that could not be obtained on the same question is a missing precondition. Reported as indeterminate with no anomaly asserted.
findings.assumptions: Both numbers (9 and 93) are stated verbatim in the same paragraph, so no bound was assumed. This entry is recorded for transparency about a Stage-1 `impossible` that did not survive triage, not as evidence against the paper; the sweep itself judged the consequence to be nil.
findings.plain: The paper says 9 of its 93 patients dropped out and calls that 9.6%. Worked as a share of 93 that figure would be 9.7%, so one of our checks called the printed number impossible. The independent reference implementation we are required to confirm such claims against did not agree, because it cannot test percentages and tested a different question instead. Since we could not get a matching second opinion, we report no problem here. Nothing in the paper's conclusions depends on this figure either way.

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected; this records a Stage-1 finding withdrawn at triage because the required cross-check could not be obtained on the same question.

findings.title: Multiplicity across 44 omnibus tests and 132 pairwise comparisons not computable
findings.location: Supplementary Annex 1 and Results, final paragraph
findings.reported: "Given the low sample size of the trial that would inherently lead to the low power of reported analyses, no further hypothesis testing was performed." Bonferroni is applied only within each outcome's three pairwise comparisons.
findings.computed: Not computed. multiplicity_report returned n_tests = 0 for a fully-formed 22-test intention-to-treat payload submitted in this pass, reproducing the payload-parsing defect the sweep recorded; family-wise error rate, the four correction thresholds and the surviving-claims interval are therefore unavailable, and no hand arithmetic was substituted. What can be stated from reading alone: the paper performs at least 48 omnibus tests (22 intention-to-treat and 22 per-protocol in the annex, plus 2 composite and 2 safety in the text) and reports 132 supplementary pairwise comparisons, with nothing correcting across the 22 outcome-by-timepoint families or across the two analysis populations. Two of 22 intention-to-treat omnibus tests fall below 0.05, close to the roughly 1.1 expected by chance. Separately, the Results claim that "no further hypothesis testing was performed" is contradicted by the tests reported in the supplement.
findings.assumptions: This is a defect in our tooling, not a property of the paper. The multiplicity burden most likely argues AGAINST reading the one significant Digit Span Backward result as real, so on this axis the uncorrected testing works against the paper's positive signal rather than manufacturing one.
findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label 'Individual cognitive outcome scales, ITT, Kruskal-Wallis omnibus' --tests '[{"id":"dsb_v2","p_value":0.02649,"test_type":"other","location":"SI Annex 1","correction_applied":"none"},{"id":"tmt1_v2","p_value":0.04012,"test_type":"other","location":"SI Annex 1","correction_applied":"none"}]'
findings.plain: The study ran at least 48 group comparisons and reported 132 more. It adjusted for multiple testing only in small pockets -- within each individual test's three group-to-group comparisons -- and not across the outcomes or the two ways it analysed the data. We could not calculate how many of its results would survive a proper adjustment, because the tool that does that arithmetic failed on our own input, and we did not substitute a hand calculation. Note the direction: this many comparisons makes the one significant memory-test result more likely to be a fluke, not less, so it counts against the paper's positive signal rather than for it. The paper also states that no further hypothesis testing was performed, which its own supplement contradicts.

consequence.explanation: The number of claims surviving correction could not be computed, and that count bears directly on how the one Bonferroni-surviving subscale result should be read.

findings.title: Raw-data duplication verdict unobtainable under correct column exclusions
findings.location: Linked replication dataset (Harvard Dataverse DOFCIV), sheet 'ITT_analysis set'
findings.reported: "Replication data for this analysis is published in the Harvard Dataverse, accessible at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/DOFCIV." The sheet holds one row per intention-to-treat patient across roughly 120 columns and 7,738 numeric cells.
findings.computed: The tool returned `highly_suspicious` with 2,260 duplicated row pairs, which the sweep deliberately downgraded to indeterminate, and I uphold that downgrade. Three reasons. The exclude_columns argument did not take effect (n_columns_excluded = 0 on two attempts in different formats), so the verdict was computed with subject ID, group code, sex and six date columns included -- all of which repeat across patients by design. 2,260 of the 3,655 possible pairs among 86 patients is roughly 62% of the entire pair space, which is a saturation signature rather than a duplication signature; genuine copy-paste is rare and localised. And the sheet is a wide table of bounded low-cardinality cognitive scores alongside z-score transforms of those same columns, so every raw-score collision is counted again in its derived column. input.report_markdown:
This is a phase II, single-centre, three-arm randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 93 patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, conducted in Cluj-Napoca between April 2018 and September 2021. It asks whether adding repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to Cerebrolysin improves cognition beyond Cerebrolysin alone, and beyond placebo. The primary endpoint is a composite z-score of change from baseline across ten neurocognitive instruments, assessed at Day 101 and Day 180 and analysed non-parametrically (Kruskal-Wallis, with Dunn post-hoc tests and Bonferroni adjustment). The authors conclude that the combination is safe and well tolerated, that no primary outcome reached statistical significance, and that descriptive trends favour both active arms.

## What verified

The arithmetic this paper does print is in good order. Every participant-flow relation reconciles exactly: the three composite subgroups sum to 64, the per-arm adverse-event counts sum to the stated 21, the intention-to-treat population plus the seven excluded patients equals the 93 enrolled, the per-protocol population plus the two named losses equals the intention-to-treat set, and the COVID visit delays sum to 16. Every Bonferroni relation in both main tables that is not capped at 1 reproduces at the printed precision, with a largest discrepancy of one part in ten million -- confirming three comparisons per family and that the adjustment was applied as described. Both tables typed at 100% coverage with no ambiguous cells. That is what a carefully prepared results section looks like, and it is worth saying plainly.

It also has to be said what that coverage does not extend to. This paper reports no group means, no standard deviations and no confidence intervals for any outcome -- results appear only as chi-squared values, Dunn Z statistics and p-values. The entire granularity family of checks (GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT, SPRITE) therefore has nothing to work on, not because the paper passed them but because it reports no quantity they apply to. Eleven summation relations, one power calculation and thirty-six typed cells is the real extent of what could be recomputed against a paper reporting 291 statistics.

## Why the headline problem is the one it is

Three considerations put the Day-180 p-value first. It sits on a co-primary endpoint, which the safety findings and the reporting gaps do not. It is contradicted by the paper's own supplementary material rather than by any assumption we supplied. And the contradiction is corroborated twice over: the companion Day-101 figure is internally consistent, which rules out a systematic problem with how these tests were run, and Table 2's Day-180 post-hoc contrast of P.unadj = 0.02578002 is simply not compatible with an omnibus p of 0.54.

The likeliest cause is a dropped decimal point, and it should be read that way until the authors say otherwise. It is worth noting that the error runs in the direction of understating the authors' own result -- as does the discrepancy over Digit Span Backward, where the paper denies a significant subscale finding that its annex reports. A paper shading its numbers in its own favour looks different from this.

## Where the reporting, rather than the arithmetic, is the problem

The recurring pattern is that this trial is difficult to check because of what it omits. A three-arm randomised trial reported under CONSORT gives no baseline characteristics table, no per-arm randomised or analysis-population sizes, and no registration number. Twenty-two intention-to-treat patients -- 26% of that population -- are absent from the primary composite analysis, attributed only to "missing data", and cannot be located by arm. Three of ten stated co-primary instruments feed the composite score and are never reported individually. A stratified analysis is pre-specified, its triggering condition is reported in the Discussion, and it never appears.

None of these is an anomaly in the sense of a number that cannot be right. Together they mean that the checks which would ordinarily carry the most weight on a randomised trial -- baseline similarity across arms, per-arm proportion reconstruction, effect-size plausibility against external benchmarks -- had no input at all. That is a hole in this review, not a clean result, and it should not be read as one.

## What remains genuinely unresolved

Two things. Whether the Day-180 figure is a typesetting slip or an error in the analysis itself cannot be settled from the published record; only the authors can say. And whether the two mislabelled Stroop columns in the Visit-3 block of the deposited dataset hold six-month or three-month values matters, because those columns feed the six-month composite -- but the column names alone establish a labelling defect, not duplicated content, and the raw-data scan found no repeated column sequences. Both are one-line answers for the authors and neither presupposes anything went wrong.

The published dataset deserves acknowledgement. Making participant-level data available is what allowed the column-naming problem to be seen at all, and it is more than most trials of this size provide.

Overall: the numbers this paper prints are largely consistent with each other, but several of its stated conclusions are not consistent with its own supplementary material, and too much of the trial is unreported for its central claims to be independently verified. The efficacy and safety conclusions warrant clarification rather than acceptance as they stand.
